definition: A certain bird; (S, O, K;) [app. a species of owl; accord. to Dmr, as cited by Freytag, a bird that roves about by night and does not sleep; and hence rendered by him, and by Golius, strix. No other...
sourceDefinition: A certain bird; (S, O, K;) [app. a species of owl; accord. to Dmr, as cited by Freytag, a bird that roves about by night and does not sleep; and hence rendered by him, and by Golius, strix. No other meaning of the word, as an appellative, is mentioned in the S.] ― -b2- And A certain insect that rests not all the day, going about, or going about quickly, (O, K, TA,) or, as they used to assert in the Time of Ignorance, that never rests, (TA,) moving about on the surface of water. (KL.) Mohammad Ibn-El-Mustaneer, (K, TA,) the grammarian, (TA,) was surnamed quTorub because he used to go early in the morning to Seebaweyh; so that the latter, whenever he opened his door, found him there; wherefore he said to him, maA A^anota A_il~aA quTorubu layolK [ Thou art none other than a kutrub of night ]. (K, * TA.) It is also expl. in the K as meaning Light, or active; and Th mentions that it signifies thus; and adds that one says, A_in~ahu laquTorubu layolK [ Verily he is a kutrub of night ]; but this shows that it means an insect [described above], and is not [properly speaking] an epithet. (TA.) To this insect is likened a man who labours during the day in accomplishing worldly wants and in the evening is fatigued so that he sleeps during the night until he enters upon the time of morning to betake himself to the like thereof, h`*aA jiyfapu layoli quTorubu nahaArK [lit. This is a corpse of the night, a kutrub of the day ]. (O, from an explanation of a trad.) [See also Freytag's Arab. Prov. i. 329 and 643.] ― -b3- And [hence, app.,] (assumed tropical:) A thief who is skilful, or active, in thievishness: (O, M, TA:) for All~iS~u AlfaArihu fiY All~uSuwSiy~api , an explanation of AlquTorubu given [in the O and] by IM and others, the copies of the K erroneously substitute All~iSu waAlfaA^orapu [as though quTorubN had the significations of a thief and a rat or mouse ]. (TA.) ― -b4- And The male (Lth, O, K, TA) of the [ kind of demon called ] siEolaAp (Lth, TA) or of the guwl [which is said to signify the same as sElAp ]; as also ↓ quToruwbN . (O, K, TA.) ― -b5- And [app. A young, or little, jinnee: thus quroTubN is expl. in the L: or] the young ones, or little ones, of the jinn. (K.) ― -b6- And A young, or little, dog: (O:) or the young ones, or little ones, of dogs. (K.) ― -b7- And A wolf such as is termed A^amoEaT [i. e. whose hair has fallen off, part after part, or has become scanty; or mischievous, or malignant ]. (O, K.) ― -b8- And An ignorant person, (O, K, TA,) who boasts by reason of his ignorance ( yaZoharu bijaholihi ). (O, TA.) ― -b9- And Cowardly, or a coward, (O, K, TA,) even if intelligent. (O, TA.) ― -b10- And Lightwitted; syn. safiyhN ; (O, K, TA;) as also ↓ quToruwbN : and IAar has mentioned as a pl. in this sense, used by a poet, qaTaAriybu , which, ISd says, may be pl. of quToruwbN or of a sing. of some other form requiring such a form of pl., or it may be used as a pl. of quTorubN by poetic license. (TA.) ― -b11- And Thrown down, or prostrated, on the ground, syn. maSoruwEN , (O, K, TA,) by reason of diabolical possession or wrestling. (O, * TA.) -A2- Also A species of melancholia; (O, K, TA;) a well-known disease, arising from the black bile; (TA;) mostly originating in the month of $ubaAT [ February, O. S. ]; vitiating, or disordering, the intellect, contracting the face, occasioning continual unhappiness, causing to wander about in the night, and rendering the face A^axoDar [here app. meaning of a dark, or an ashy, dust-colour ], the eyes sunken, and the body emaciated. (O.) [A more ample discription is given by Avicenna (Ibn-Seenà). in book iii. pp. 315, et seq. SM states that he had not found this in any other lexicon than the K. Golius explains the word as signifying Lycanthropia, on the authority of Rhazes (Er-Rázee).]

definition: A kind of glove;
sourceDefinition: A kind of glove; a thing which is made for the two hands, or hands and arms, stuffed with cotton, (S, L, K,) and having buttons which are buttoned upon the fore arms, (S, L,) worn by a woman as a protection from the cold; (S, L, K;) they are made of skins, and of felt; are worn by the women of the Arabs of the desert; and extend to the bones of the elbow: (L, TA:) a pair of them is called quf~aAzaAni : (S, L:) or a thing which the women of the Arabs of the desert make for themselves, stuffed with cotton, covering a woman's two hands, with her fingers, and, some add, having buttons upon the fore arm; like what the carrier of the falcon wears: (Msb:) or a thing which those women make for themselves, covering the fingers and hand and arm: and a thing which the sportsman [meaning the falconer ] wears upon each hand, or hand and arm, of skin, or of felt, or wool: (Mgh:) or a kind of women's ornament for the hands and feet, or the hands and arms and the feet and legs: and a reticulated iron thing ( HadiydapN mu$ab~akapN , accord. to the TA, as from the K, but in the CK mu$otabikapN ,) upon which the falcon sits. (K.) ― -b2- And [hence,] Whiteness in the A^a$aAEir [or hairs next the hoof ] of a horse. (K. [See also qafiza , and quf~aza , and A^aqofazu .])

definition: A kind of A^aqiT ;
sourceDefinition: A kind of A^aqiT ; what rises ( from the milk ) above the water, the latter becoming clear beneath it; or what becomes thick, or coagulated, its oily matter floating upon the surface, ( yakovaA^u ,) in the pot, and is poured out; the upper part whereof is gross, or thick. So says AHát; and he adds, What is termed mSrE [evidently, I think, a mistranscription for muDar~iEN ,] is what becomes thick, or coagulated, and almost thoroughly cooked: EAqd is that of which the water has gone, and which is thoroughly cooked: kariyS is that which is cooked with nahoq or HamaSiyS : maSol is a kind of AqT cooked again: and vawor is a great piece of it. (TA.)

definition: The rope that is tied to the bucket after the maniyn , which is the first [or main ] rope, so that it ( the krb ) remains if the mnyn break: or the rope that is tied to the middle of the cross-bars...
sourceDefinition: The rope that is tied to the bucket after the maniyn , which is the first [or main ] rope, so that it ( the krb ) remains if the mnyn break: or the rope that is tied to the middle of the cross-bars of the bucket, ( and is then doubled, and then trebled, S,) so as to be that which is next the water, in order that the great rope may not rot: (S, K:) but in a marginal note in a copy of the S, it is said that this latter explanation properly applies to the darak ; not to the krb : (IM:) pl. A^akoraAbN . (TA.) -A2- karabN [coll. gen. n.] The lower parts, or ends, of palm-branches, (S, K,) which are thick and broad, (K,) like shoulderblades: (S:) or the stumps of the branches, or what remain upon the palm-tree, of the lower parts, or ends, of the branches, after the lopping, like steps: n. un. with p . (TA.) Hence the proverb, mataY kaAna Hukomu All~`hi fiY karabi Aln~axoli [ When was the wisdom of God in the stumps, or lower ends, of palm-branches? ] (S.) Said by Jereer, in reply to Es-Salatán El-'Abdee, who had pronounced El-Ferezdak superior to Jereer in point of lineage, and Jereer superior to ElFerezdak as a poet. IB denies it to be a proverb; but IM contends against him that it is, [The meaning is, When was God's wisdom in husbandmen, and possessors of palm-trees? for the region of Es-Salatán's tribe abounded in palm-trees. The words are applied to a man who provokes another to a contest for excellence, being unworthy of the contest. See Freytag, Arab. Prov., ii. 628.]

sourceDefinition: (S, K) and ↓ karaAbapN (K), but the former is the more approved word, (TA,) Dates that are picked from among the roots of the branches (S, K) after the racemes of fruit have been cut off: (S:) the scattered dates that remain at the roots of the branches: (AHn, TA voce xulaAlapN , which signifies the same:) pl. A^akoribapN , in the formation of which, the augmentative letter (meaning the fem. p , TA,) seems to have been rejected [or disregarded]; for fuEaAlapN (this is the right reading; TA; but in some copies of the K we read fuEaAlaY , and in others fuEaAl ;) does not form a pl. on the measure A^afoEilapN . He also says, in one place, that Akrbp is [said to be] pl. of krAbp , which signifies “ dates that fall among the roots of the palm-branches; ” but [that] this is a mistake: upon which ISd remarks, In like manner, [this] his saying is in my opinion a mistake. (TA.)

A_iloqaAHN , [and quasi-inf. n. laqaAHN , q. v.; et vide infra;] and ↓ lq~HhA , inf. n. taloqiyHN ; (S, Msb, A, K;) and ↓ laqaHahaA , inf. n. laqoHN ; (K;) (tropical:) He fecundated the palm-tree by means of the ↓ laqaAH , or spadix of the male tree, which is bruised, or brayed, and sprinkled [ upon the spadix of the female ]: (A:) or, by inserting a stalk of a raceme of the male tree into the spathe [ of the female, after shaking off the pollen of the former upon the spadix of the female; for such is the general practice]: this is done in the following manner: you leave the spathe of the [female] palm-tree two or three nights after its bursting open: then you take a stalk of a raceme of the male tree, which is best if old, of the preceding year, and insert it into the spadix [of the female, after shaking off the pollen, as above mentioned]; and this you do according to a certain measure: it should not be done but by a man acquainted with the manner of proceeding in this case; for if he be ignorant, and do too much, he turns the spathe, and mars it; and if he do too little, many of the dates produced will be without stones; and if he do it not at all to the palm-tree, he will derive no advantage from the spadix thereof that year: (L:) ↓ laqaHN is the name of that which is taken from the male palm-tree ( AlfuH~aAl : so in the L: in the K, AlfaHol :) to be inserted in the other, [ namely the spathe of the female ]. (L, K.) [See also laqaAHN . (A.) ― -b6- Aln~aZaru fiY EawaAqibi A@loA^umwuri A@loEuquwli ↓ taloqiyHu (tropical:) [ Consideration of the results, or issues, of things is ( a means of ) fecundation of the intellects ]. A_iloqaAHN , [and quasi-inf. n. laqaAHN , q. v.; et vide infra;] and ↓ lq~HhA , inf. n. taloqiyHN ; (S, Msb, A, K;) and ↓ laqaHahaA , inf. n. laqoHN ; (K;) (tropical:) He fecundated the palm-tree by means of the ↓ laqaAH , or spadix of the male tree, which is bruised, or brayed, and sprinkled [ upon the spadix of the female ]: (A:) or, by inserting a stalk of a raceme of the male tree into the spathe [ of the female, after shaking off the pollen of the former upon the spadix of the female; for such is the general practice]: this is done in the following manner: you leave the spathe of the [female] palm-tree two or three nights after its bursting open: then you take a stalk of a raceme of the male tree, which is best if old, of the preceding year, and insert it into the spadix [of the female, after shaking off the pollen, as above mentioned]; and this you do according to a certain measure: it should not be done but by a man acquainted with the manner of proceeding in this case; for if he be ignorant, and do too much, he turns the spathe, and mars it; and if he do too little, many of the dates produced will be without stones; and if he do it not at all to the palm-tree, he will derive no advantage from the spadix thereof that year: (L:) ↓ laqaHN is the name of that which is taken from the male palm-tree ( AlfuH~aAl : so in the L: in the K, AlfaHol :) to be inserted in the other, [ namely the spathe of the female ]. (L, K.) [See also laqaAHN . (L.) ― -b3- A^aloqaHati Alr~iyHu Als~aHaAba (S) (tropical:) The wind impregnated, or fecundated, the cloud, or clouds; (L;) and in like manner, AlqHt Alr~iyaAHu Al$~ajara wanaHowahu [ The winds fecundated the trees ] (K) [ and the like ]. (A.) ― -b5- Eaqolahu ↓ jar~aba AlA^umuwra falaq~aHato (tropical:) [ He became experienced in affairs, and they fecundated his intellect ]. (A.) ― -b6- Aln~aZaru fiY EawaAqibi A@loA^umwuri A@loEuquwli ↓ taloqiyHu (tropical:) [ Consideration of the results, or issues, of things is ( a means of ) fecundation of the intellects ]. (A.) ― -b7- laA tuloqiHo siloEataka biAlA^ayomaAni (tropical:) [ Make not thy merchandise productive of a high price by means of oaths ]. (A.)

definition: The semen genitale (L, K) of a stallion camel, and horse, and (tropical:) of a man.
sourceDefinition: The semen genitale (L, K) of a stallion camel, and horse, and (tropical:) of a man. (L.) I'Ab, being asked respecting a man who had two wives, one of whom suckled a boy, and the other a girl, [not his own children,] whether the boy might marry the girl, answered “ No; because the lqAH [i. e., liqaAH or ↓ laqaAH , as shown below,] is one: ” meaning, says Lth, that the semen genitale which impregnated them both, and which was the source of the milk of both, was one, and that the two sucklings had thus become as though they were the children of the two women's husband: but, says Az, lqAH may here be a quasi-inf. n., syn. with A_iloqaAHN ; like EaTaA='N and A_iEoTaA='N &c.: (L:) [and the like is said in the Msb.] ↓ laqaAHN and liqaAHN , with fet-h and kesr, are substs. from A^aloqaHa , [q. v.] syn. with A_iloqaAHN , signifying impregnation, or the getting with young; and so in the answer of I'Ab above mentioned. (Msb.)

definition: A camel (S, K) itself: (S:) pl.
sourceDefinition: A camel (S, K) itself: (S:) pl. liqaAHN . (S, K.) ― -b2- See laAqiHN . ― -b3- laquwHN and ↓ liqoHapN (S, Msb, K) and ↓ laqoHapN , (Msb, K,) applied to a she-camel, i. q. HaluwbN [meaning Milch, and a milch camel ]: (S, Msb, K:) but Az says, that the former only is used as an epithet; you say nAqp laquwHN , and not nAqpN liqoHapN , but h`*ihi liqoHapN fulaAnK : (TA:) or laquwHN is [an epithet] applied to a she-camel during the first two or three months after her having brought forth; and after this she is termed labuwnN : (AA, S, K:) and accord. to some, ↓ liqoHapN signifies a milch camel abounding with milk: or a she-camel from the time when the hump of her young one becomes fat, until the expiration of seven months, when she weans her young one, and this she does at the [auroral] rising of Canopus: (TA:) [which rising, in central Arabia, about the commencement of the era of the Flight was between the 30th of July and the 12th of August:] also ↓ liqoHapN and ↓ laqoHapN a she-camel that has lately brought forth: (L:) pl. of laquwHN , liqaAHN (S, Msb, K) and laqaAy^iHu ; (ISh;) and pl. of ↓ liqoHapN (and of ↓ laqoHapN , K, TA,) liqaHN (S, Msb, K) and liqaAHN . (ISh, Th, Msb.) ― -b4- The Arabs also said liqaAHaAni A^asowadaAni [ Two black herds of milch camels ], like as they said qaTiyEaAni ; for they said liqaAHN waAHidapN in like manner as they said qaTiyEN waAHidN and A_ibilN waAHidapN . (S.) ― -b5- Almusolimiyna ↓ A^adir~uwA liqoHapa (tropical:) Milk ye the milch camel of the Muslims: occurring in a trad., alluding to the tribute ( faYo' and xaraAj ) whence were derived the stipends and fixed appointments of the persons addressed, and to the collecting it with equity. (TA.)

definition: (IAar, S, K) and ↓ laquwHN (K) and ↓ maloquwHapN (Msb) A she-camel having just conceived, or become pregnant;
sourceDefinition: (IAar, S, K) and ↓ laquwHN (K) and ↓ maloquwHapN (Msb) A she-camel having just conceived, or become pregnant; (IAar, K;) as also qaAriHN : afterwards, when her pregnancy has become manifestly apparent, she is termed xalifapN : (IAar:) pl. of the former lawaAqiHu (K) and luq~aHN ; (TA;) and of the second, luquHN . (L, K, TA: in the CK luq~aHN .) ― -b2- riyaAHN lawaAqiHu (S, K, &c.,) (tropical:) Pregnant winds; so called because they bear the water and the clouds, and turn the latter over and about, and then cause them to send down rain; (TA;) or because they become pregnant, and then impregnate the clouds: (IJ:) the sing. is riyHN laAqiHN , the contr. of which is termed riyHN EaqiymN [or “ a barren wind ”]: (ISd:) or ryH lAqH signifies *aAtu laqalaAHK [ possessing that which impregnates ]; like as dirohamN waAzinN signifies *uw wazoni ; rajulN raAmiHN , *uw rumoHK : (AHeyth:) or ryAH lwAqH signifies impregnating, or fecundating, winds; (S, K;) as also ↓ malaAqiHu [pl. of muloqiHapN ]: (K:) or it is not allowable to say malaAqiHu ; (S;) but this is the regular form of the word; because the wind impregnates the clouds; (IJ;) and thus lwAqH is extr.: or, as some say, the proper original word is muloqiHapN ; but the winds do not impregnate unless they are themselves pregnant; as though they were pregnant with good, and, when they raised the clouds, transmitted to them that good. (S.) ― -b3- HarobN laAqiHN (K) (tropical:) War pregnant [ with great events. ] (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , inf. n. tamoHiySN , He rendered it clear, pure, free from every admixture or imperfection or the like; as also ↓ maHaSahu , aor. , inf. n. maHoSN . (Az, A, TA.) You say, maH~aSa Al*~ahaba , (A, TA,) or ↓ maHaSahu , (S, K,) He cleared, or purified, the gold from what was mixed with it, (S, A, K,) i. e. from the earth, or dust, and dirt, (TA,) biAln~aAri by fire. (S, A, K.) ― -b2- [Hence,] (tropical:) He (God) purged, or purified it; namely a man's heart: and him; namely a man repenting. (A.) It is said in the Kur, [iii. 135,] waliyumaH~iSa A@ll~`hu A@l~a*iyna A@manuwA (tropical:) And that God may purify those who believe: (TA:) or purge away the sins of those who believe: (Fr, TA:) or these words have another meaning, which see below. (TA.) It is also said in a trad., mentioning a sedition, or conflict and faction, or the like, yumaH~aSu Aln~aAsu fiyhaA kamaA yumaH~aSu *ahabu AlmaEodini , i.e. (tropical:) Men shall be cleared therein, one from another, like as the gold from the mine is cleared from the earth, or dust. (TA.) tamoHiySu Al*~unuwbi signifies (tropical:) The purging of sins. (TA.) And you say, maH~iSo Ean~aA *unuwbanaA , meaning (tropical:) Remove thou, or put thou away, from us our sins. (TA.) [But this phrase may be rendered somewhat differently; as will be seen below.] And A@ll~`hu maA bika ↓ maHaSa , and maH~aSahu ; i.e. (tropical:) May God remove, or put away, what is in thee. (TA.) ― -b3- [Hence, also,] (assumed tropical:) He tried, proved, or tested, him: (S, IAth, K:) and accord. to Ibn-'Arafeh, the verb has this meaning in the phrase quoted above from the Kur: [but he adds,] because the trial of the Muslims diminishes their sins: for (TA) tamoHySN also signifies The diminishing [a thing]. (Ibn- 'Arafeh, K.) You say, maH~aSa A@ll~`hu Eanoka *unuwbaka May God diminish thy sins. (TA.) ― -b4- And the clearing, or cleansing, flesh from sinews, (K, TA,) for the purpose of twisting them into a bow-string. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , inf. n. maTarN , [ The sky, or, as it sometimes means, the rain, ] rained; as also ↓ A^amoTarat : (T, S, Msb:) but the former is said to relate to that which is sent in mercy, and the latter to that which is sent in punishment. (Msb.) See also what follows. ― -b2- [Both are also trans. You say,] maTaratohumu Als~amaA='u , (A, K,) aor. , (TA,) inf. n. maTorN and maTarN ; (K:) and ↓ A^amoTaratohum , (A, TA,) which latter is the worse form, [as will be seen below,] The sky rained upon them. (A, K, TA.) And muTironaA We were rained upon; we had rain. (S. TA,) ― -b3- You say also, maTarahumo xayorN , and $ar~N , (tropical:) [ Good, and evil, poured upon them; or betided them ]. (A.) And maTaraniY bixayorK (tropical:) He did good to me. (K.) And maA maTaraniY bixayorK (tropical:) [ He did not any good to me ]. (A.) And maA muTira minohu xayorFA , [in the CK, incorrectly, xayorN ,] and bixayorK , (tropical:) Good did not betide him from him, or it. (K, TA.) But ↓ A^amoTarahumu A@ll~`hu is only said in relation to punishment: (K, TA:) as in the saying in the Kur, [xxvi. 173, and xxvii. 59,] Ealayohimo ↓ waA^amoTaronaA maTarFA fasaA='a maTaru A@lomuno*ariyna (tropical:) [ And we rained upon them a rain, and evil was the rain of the warned people]: and again in the Kur, [xv. 74,] Ealayohimo HijaArapF mino sij~iylK ↓ waA^amoTaronaA (tropical:) [ And we rained upon them stones of baked clay ]: the stones being regarded as rain because of their descent from the sky: some, however, hold that maTara and ↓ A^amaTara are the same in meaning. (TA.) -A2- mar~a Alfarasu yamoTuru , inf. n. maTorN (S, A) and ↓ muTuwrN ; (S;) and ↓ yatamaT~aru ; (S, A;) (tropical:) The horse passed, or went, running vehemently, like the pouring of rain: (A:) or went quickly; or hastened; (S;) as also maTara Alfarasu , (K,) aor. as above, (TA,) and so the inf. ns.: (K:) or this last signifies the horse was quick in his passing, or going, and in his running; and so ↓ tmT~r . (TA.) You say also, bihi farasuhu ↓ tamaT~ara (A, TA) (tropical:) His horse ran, and hastened, or went quickly, with him. (TA.) And maTarati AlT~ayoru , and ↓ tmT~rt , (tropical:) The birds hastened, or were quick, in their descent. (K.) And Alxayolu ↓ tmT~rt (tropical:) The horses came, (K, TA,) and went, quickly, (TA,) outstripping one another. (K, TA.) ― -b2- maTara fiY AlA^aroDi , inf. n. muTuwrN ; and ↓ tmT~r ; (tropical:) He (a man) went away in, or into, the country, or land; (S, K;) and hastened; as also qaTara . (TA, art. qTr .) ― -b3- *ahaba AlbaEiyru famaA A^adoriY mano maTara bihi (S, K *) (tropical:) [ The camel has gone away, and I know not who has gone with it, or] has taken it: (K:) and in like manner, *ahaba vawobiY Alx (tropical:) my garment has gone, &c. (TA.)

definition: , (S, K,) pronounced with ' in the dial.
sourceDefinition: , (S, K,) pronounced with ' in the dial. of the people of Mekkeh, (S,) whose pronunciation of it is disapproved by Sb on account of its uncommonness; (TA;) by others, nabiY~N , without ' ; (S, K, TA;) A prophet: (TA:) of the measure faEiylN used in the sense of the measure mufoEl [i. e. mufoEilN or mafoEalN ] (IB) or faAEilN (S, Es-Sunoosee) or mafoEuwlN ; (Es-Sunoosee) i. e., who acquaints or informs mankind, (S, K, TA,) or who is acquainted or informed, respecting God and things unseen: or accord. to some, it is derived from nabowapN and nabaAwapN signifying “ elevation; ” (see art. nbw ;) in which case it is originally without ' : or, accord. to others, from nabiYo'N in a sense given below; that of “ a conspicuous way. ” (TA.) It is a less special word than rasuwlN [when thereby is meant an apostle of God]; for every rswl is a nbY~ , but not every nbY~ is a rswl . (TA.) Pl. A^anobiyaA='u (S, K, without ' , because the ' is changed into Y in the sing., S,) and nubaA^='u (S, K, like kuramaA='u [pl. of kariymN ] TA,) and A^anobaA='N [K, these two preserving the original radical ' ] and nabiy~uwna , (K,) without ' : (TA:) but some pronounced the first and last of these pls., in the Kur-án, with ' ; though the more approved pronunciation is without ' . (TA.) The dim. is nubay~y^N , (S, K,) with those who make the pl. nubaA^='N [or A^anobaA='N ]; but with those who make the pl. A^anobiyaA=' , it is nubaY~N . (K.) ― -b2- An Arab of the desert said to Mohammad, yaA nabiYo'a All~`hi , and the latter disapproved of his pronouncing nbY' in this case with ' , because, as it signifies An emigrant, he meant thereby to call him an emigrant from Mekkeh to El-Medeeneh. (S, K, TA.) ― -b3- nabiYo'N A conspicuous, an evident, or a clear, way. (K.) Hence, accord. to some, the apostle [or rather prophet] is so called, because he is the conspicuous, evident, way, that conducts to God. (MF.) ― -b4- nabiYo'N and ↓ naAbiy^N An elevated, or a protuberant, or gibbous, place. (K.) ― -b5- Hence it is said in a trad., laA tuSal~uwA EalaY Aln~abiYo'i [ Pray not upon the place that is elevated, or protuberant ]. (K.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. , (S, Msb,) inf. n. najo$N , (S, Msb, K,) He concealed himself. (Msb.) -A2- [And hence, He pursued game, or objects of the chase: (see naAji$N :) or] he roused game, or objects of the chase, (S, Mgh, K,) and scared them from place to place. (TA.) You say also, naja$uwA Ealayohi AlS~ayoda , meaning, They scared the chase, or game, towards him, and drove and collected it to him. (TA.) ― -b2- He searched after a thing, and roused it. (Sh, A'Obeyd, K.) This, accord. to Sh, is the primary signification: [but accord. to Fei, the primary signification is the first given above:] and hence the saying in a trad., laA taToluEu Al$~amosu Hat~aY tanojusuhaA val`vumiAy^apK wasit~uwna malakFA The sun does not rise until three hundred and sixty angels rouse it. (TA.) ― -b3- He drew forth, educed, or elicited. (K.) ― -b4- He collected together (S, K) camels [&c.] after a state of dispersion. (S.) ― -b5- He drove vehemently. (TA.) -A3- naja$a , aor. , (Msb, TA,) inf. n. najo$N (S, A, Mgh, Msb, K) and naja$N , [which is the form generally used by the professors of practical law,] (ISh, Mgh, Sgh, TA,) or this is a simple subst., (Msb,) He demanded the sale of an article of merchandise for more than its price, (A, Mgh, Msb,) not meaning to purchase it, (Mgh, Msb,) in order that another might see him and fall into the snare thus laid for him: and in like manner it is used with respect to marriage, [i. e., with respect to dowers,] and other things: (A, Mgh, Msb:) and the doing thus is forbidden: (Mgh:) it is from naja$a signifying “ he roused ” game: (Mgh:) or from the same verb signifying “ he concealed himself; ” because he who does so conceals his intention: (Msb:) or he augmented the price of an article of merchandise, not desiring to purchase it, but in order that another might hear him and augment in the same manner: (A'Obeyd, L:) or he outbade in a sale, in order that another might fall into a snare, he himself not wanting the thing: (S:) or he augmented the price of an article of merchandise, or praised it, in order that another might see that, and be deceived by him: (Ibráheem El-Harbee:) or he praised an article of merchandise belonging to another in order that he might sell it, or dispraised it in order that it might not be easy for him to sell it: (ISh:) or he concurred with a man desiring to sell a thing, by praising him: (Abu-l-Khattáb, K:) or he bargained with a man desiring to sell a thing, offering him a large price, in order that another might see him and fall into a snare: or he scared people from one thing to another: (K:) also, he praised a thing; or praised it exceedingly, or for that which was not in it, or excessively and falsely; syn. madaHa $ayoy^FA and A^aToraAhu : and he invented, or forged, a lie. (TA.) It is said in a trad., (S,) ↓ laA tanaAja$uwA , (S, Mgh, Msb,) i. e., Ye shall not practise najo$ , or naja$ : (Mgh, Msb:) or ↓ tanaAju$N signifies the bidding one against another, successively increasing their offers, in a sale, or other case; (K;) for it sometimes signifies the doing so in the case of a dowry, in order that the doing so may be heard, and the amount may consequently be augmented: (TA:) and Sh mentions, with respect to ↓ tanaAju$N , on the authority of Aboo-Sa'eed, another thing, which is allowable, namely, [that it signifies the conspiring to promote the marriage of ] the woman who has been married and divorced time after time; and [ the sale of ] the article of merchandise that has been bought time after time and then sold. (TA.)

definition: A pursuer, or capturer, or insnarer, of game, or objects of the chase;
sourceDefinition: A pursuer, or capturer, or insnarer, of game, or objects of the chase; (Msb;) as also ↓ najiy$N and ↓ naj~aA$N ; (Ibn-'Abbád, K;) because he conceals himself: (Msb:) or [ naAji$N and] ↓ naj~aA$N and ↓ najuw$N signify one who rouses the game, or objects of the chase; (Az, TA;) and so ↓ minoja$N and ↓ minojaA$N : (L:) or naAji$N and ↓ najaA$iY~N (Akh, K) [and ↓ nijaA$iY~N accord. to some copies of the K] and ↓ minojaA$N (Az, K) one who rouses them in order that they may pass by the pursuer, or capturer, or insnarer, thereof: (Akh, Az, K:) or naAji$N signifies one who scares them towards him, and drives and collects them to him: (S, A, TA:) and ↓ naj~aA$N one who drives vehemently; (TA;) or one who urges camels; (A;) or who collects them after a state of dispersion: (S:) and ↓ naj~aA$iY~N [with teshdeed to the j as well as to the Y ,] one who drives, or urges, travelling-camels and other beasts of carriage, in the market-place, to elicit their qualities of pace: (AA, TA:) and this last also signifies [absolutely] one who draws forth, or elicits, a thing. (A'Obeyd, TA.) -A2- Also, One who practises najo$ , or naja$ , in an affair of buying and selling: (Msb, TA: *) [see 1:] and ↓ naj~aA$N one who does so much, or often. (Msb.)

Sad~aqa and ka*~aba in the Msb. ― -b9- nasabahu A_ilaY ka*aA (tropical:) He referred its origin, or the origin or derivation of its name, to such a thing. ― -b10- He attributed, or ascribed, it to such a thing. ― -b11- ] nasabahu A_ilaY fulaAnK He named him, or called him, in relation, or reference, to such a one; meaning an ancestor: and in like manner, in relation, or reference, to a tribe, a town or district, an art or trade, &c. See nisobapN . ― -b12- nasabahu A_laY k*aA (tropical:) He named it, or called it, in relation, or reference, to such a thing. ― -b13- nasaba A_ilayohi ka*aA , and, by inversion, nasabahu A_ilaY ka*aA , (see S and K, in art. jhl , &c.) (tropical:) He attributed or imputed to him, or charged him with, or accused him of, such a thing; namely, a fault &c. Both phrases are often used as signifying thus by classical writers, and in the present day.] ― -b14- nasaba biAlomaroA^api , (S, K,) aor. , (S,) and , (L,) inf. n. nasiybN (S, K) and nasabN and manosabapN , (K,) i. q. $ab~aba bihaA ; q. v.; (S, K;) He mentioned the woman in an amatory manner, in the beginning [or prelude ] of a poem: (TA, voce $b~b :) he mentioned the woman in amatory language, in the beginning of a qaSiydap , and then turned to the object of praise: [for it is a general rule to commence a qSydp in praise of a king, or hero, or the like, with nsyb ; the transition from this is termed Alt~axal~uSu : see also AiqotaDaba :] (IKh:) he mentioned the woman in his poem, describing her as characterized by beauty and youth &c.: (Lb:) or describing her as characterized by good qualities, whether truly or falsely. (Z.) This phrase and nasaba Alr~ajula both signify description; the latter signifying “ he described the man with relation to his father, or his city or country, or the like; ” and the former phrase, he described the woman as characterized by beauty and youth and love or affection &c. (MF.) [See gazila , and gazalN .]

definition: (tropical:) Relation;
sourceDefinition: (tropical:) Relation; proportion; comparison; with respect to quantity, or measure, and the like. See nasabN . ― -b2- binisobapi ka*aA In proportion to such a thing. ― -b3- nisobapu AlEa$arapi A_ilaY AlmiAy^api The proportion of ten to a hundred is [ that of a tenth ]. (Msb.) ― -b4- [You also say biAln~isobapi A_ilaY ka*aA In relation to, or in comparison with, such a thing. ] ― -b5- nisobapN A name of relation to a father, mother, tribe, town or district, art or trade, &c.: [as EalawiY~N , faATimiY~N , qura$iY~N , mak~iY~N , jawohariY~N :] ending with Y~ . A more general name of this kind should precede a more particular one: thus you say Alqura$iY~u AlhaA$imiY~u : and it is better that a name of relation to a tribe should precede one of relation to a town or the like: thus you say Alqura$iY~u Almak~iY~u . It is said that the Arabs originally called themselves by such names only in relation to tribes; and that, when they took up their abodes in cultivated lands and in cities, they borrowed names of relation to towns and the like from the Persians and Copts. (Msb.) ― -b6- nisobapN (TA) and ↓ munaAsabapN (S, K) and ↓ tanaAsubN (TA) (tropical:) Resemblance; similarity; conformity; analogy; correspondence; suitableness; fitness. (S, K, TA.) Ex. bayona Al$~ayoy^ayoni nsbpN , and ↓ mnAsbpN , and ↓ tnAsbN , Between the two things is a resemblance, &c. bayonahumaA nsbpN qariybapN . Between them two is a near resemblance, &c. (TA.) [ nisobapN Hukomiy~apN The relation of a predicate to its subject (in books on logic).]

definition: , and Eanohu ↓ naAkibN , (tropical:) A man deviating from the right course of action &c.
sourceDefinition: , and Eanohu ↓ naAkibN , (tropical:) A man deviating from the right course of action &c. (A.) ― -b2- nakobaA'u [fem. of A^anokabu ] an epithet applied to Any wind that blows obliquely, taking a direction between [ the directions of ] two [ cardinal ] winds: (TA:) a wind that blows obliquely, deviating from the direction whence blow the right ( Alquw~am [or the cardinal ]) winds: (S:) or a [particular] wind that blows obliquely, and takes a direction between [ the directions of ] two [ cardinal ] winds; (K;) which destroys the camels and sheep &c., and restrains the rain: (TA:) or a wind that blows in a direction between that of the east, or easterly, wind, ( AlS~abaA ,) and that of the north, or northerly, wind, ( Al$~amaAl ): (AZ, K:) that between the south, or southerly, and east, or easterly, winds, being called jirobiyaA'u : (AZ:) [but see this word, and see below:] or what are termed nukobu Alr~iyaAHi [ nukobN being pl. of nkbA' ] are four: (IAar, Th, S, K:) namely, first, the nkbA'u AlS~abaA waAljanuwbi the wind that blows in a direction between that of the east, or easterly, and that of the south, or southerly, wind; also called AlA^azoyabu ; (S, K;) which is a very thirsty wind, that dries up much the leguminous plants; but Et-Tará- bulusee, in the Kf, and Mbr and IF, assert that the Azyb is the jnwb ; not its nkbA' : (TA:) second, the nkbA'u AlS~abaA waAl$~amaAli the wind that blows in a direction between that of the east, or easterly, and that of the north, or northerly, wind; also called AlS~aAbaypu , and called also ↓ Aln~ukayobAa'u , (S, K,) a diminutive meant to convey the opposite of a diminutive sense; for they find this wind to be very cold; (S;) it is very boisterous and very cold; unattended by rain or by any good: (TA:) third, the nkbA'u Al$~amaAli waAld~abuwri the wind that blows in a direction between that of the north, or northerly, and that of the west, or westerly, wind; also called AljirobiyaA'u ; and termed nay~iHapu AlA^azoyabi the opposite wind to the Azyb ; (S, K;) a cold wind; (S;) and sometimes attended by a little rain; but Ibn-El-Ajdábee asserts that the jrbyA' is the $mAl : (TA:) fourth, the nkbA'u Aljanuwbi wAld~abuwri the wind that blows in a direction between that of the south, or southerly, and that of the west, or westerly, wind; also called Alhayofu ; (in the CK, Alhayafu ;) and termed nay~iHapu Aln~ukayobAa'i the opposite wind to the nkybA' ; (S, K;) a hot wind (S) and very thirsty. (TA.) Accord. to Ibn-Kubás, the tract whence blows the nkbA' [by which he means only the wind that blows from the north-east or thereabout] is that extending between the point where rises the *iraAE [or the asterism composed of the stars α and β of Gemini, E. 33 degrees N., in central Arabia; or α and β of Canis Minor, E. 7 degrees N., in the same latitude ] and the pole-star: and the tract between the pole-star and the point where sets the *rAE is the tract whence blows the $mAl . Sh says, Each of the four [cardinal] winds has its nkbA' , which is called in relation to it: that of the SbA is that which is between it and the $mAl ; [ blowing from the north-east, or thereabout; ] and it resembles it in gentleness; sometimes having sharpness, or vehemence; but this is seldom; only once in a long space of time: that of the $mAl is that which is between it and the dbwr ; [ blowing from the north-west, or thereabout; ] and it resembles it in coldness: it is called Al$mAlu Al$~aAmiy~apu : each of them is called by the Arabs $Amy~p : that of the dbwr is that which is between it and the jnwb ; blowing from the point where sets suhayol [or Canopus; i. e., S. 29 degrees W., in the latitude of central Arabia ]; and it resembles it in its violence and boisterousness: and that of the jnwb is that which is between it and the SbA ; [ blowing from the south-east, or thereabout; ] and it is the wind most resembling it in its softness and in its gentleness in winter. (L.) The pl. of nkbA' is nukobN , as shown above. (S, K &c.) [See also tab~uwEu Al$~amosi , in art. tbE .] ― -b3- dabuwrN nkb [app. ↓ nakobN , originally an inf. n., used as an epithet, and therefore applicable without p to a fem noun] i. q. nakobAa'u ; [app., The nkbA' of the dbwr , a southwesterly wind ]. (TA.) ― -b4- A^anokabu A camel having a disease in the shoulder-joint, or in the shoulderblade, and in consequence halting: (S:) a camel that walks on one side, or inclining, or as though he walked on one side. (L.) ― -b5- faAmapN nakobaA'u An inclining pulley: and qiyamN nukobN inclining pulleys. (TA.) ― -b6- A^anokabu (assumed tropical:) Overpowering, or oppressive; unjust, or tyrannical. (S, TA.) ― -b7- Ald~ahoru A^anokabu laA yulib~u (assumed tropical:) Fortune abounds with evil accidents, or disasters, or afflictions, or calamities; i. e. it deviates much, or often, from the right course: it will not remain in one state: or, accord. to one relation, Aldhr Ankv Alx . A proverb. (TA.) -A2- A^anokabu A man not having with him a bow. (S, K.)

Accord. to Ibn-Kubás, the tract whence blows the nkbA' [by which he means only the wind that blows from the north-east or thereabout] is that extending between the point where rises the *iraAE [or the asterism composed of the stars α and β of Gemini, E. 33 degrees N., in central Arabia; or α and β of Canis Minor, E. 7 degrees N., in the same latitude ] and the pole-star: and the tract between the pole-star and the point where sets the *rAE is the tract whence blows the $mAl . Sh says, Each of the four [cardinal] winds has its nkbA' , which is called in relation to it: that of the SbA is that which is between it and the $mAl ; [ blowing from the north-east, or thereabout; ] and it resembles it in gentleness; sometimes having sharpness, or vehemence; but this is seldom; only once in a long space of time: that of the $mAl is that which is between it and the dbwr ; [ blowing from the north-west, or thereabout; ] and it resembles it in coldness: it is called Al$mAlu Al$~aAmiy~apu : each of them is called by the Arabs $Amy~p : that of the dbwr is that which is between it and the jnwb ; blowing from the point where sets suhayol [or Canopus; i. e., S. 29 degrees W., in the latitude of central Arabia ]; and it resembles it in its violence and boisterousness: and that of the jnwb is that which is between it and the SbA ; [ blowing from the south-east, or thereabout; ] and it is the wind most resembling it in its softness and in its gentleness in winter. sourceDefinition: (masc., Lh, K) The shoulder; i. e. the place of junction of the os humeri and the scapula, (S, K.) in a man &c; (ISd:) the place of junction of the os humeri and the scapula and the [ tendon called ] Habolu AlEaAtiqi , in a man and a bird and any other thing. (TA.) [It seems to be regarded by some as originally signifying “ a place of deflection: ” but] Sb denies its being a noun of place, because, were it so, it would be manokabN : he does not allow it to be included in the class of maToliEN , because this is extr. Pl. manaAkibu . rajulN $adiydu AlmanaAkibi , signifies A man having a strong shoulder: as though the sing. were applied to denote each part of the joint, and the pl. to denote the whole. (TA.) ― -b2- haz~uwA manaAkibahumo (tropical:) [ They shook their shoulderjoints; ] i. e., they rejoiced, or were joyful, or happy. (TA.) ― -b3- xiyAarukumo A^alayonukumo manaAkiba fiY AlS~alaApi (assumed tropical:) [ The best of you are the most easy of you in the shoulder-joints in prayer: ] meaning. those of you who keep [ most ] still therein: or, as some say, those who [ most readily ] give room to such as enter the rank in prayer. (TA, from a trad.) ― -b4- manokibu Alfarasi The star β in Pegasus. (El-Kazweenee &c.) ― -b5- manokibu AljawozaA'i The bright, and very great star, a, in the right shoulderjoint, of Orion. (El-Kazweenee &c.) ― -b6- manokibN (tropical:) The side of anything; or a lateral, or an adjacent, part, quarter, or tract, thereof: (K:) pl. manaAkibu : ex. sironaA fiY mnkbK mina AlA^aroDi We proceeded, or journeyed, along a side, or lateral part, of the land: and, in like manner, mina Aljabali of the mountain: (TA:) so in the Kur, lxvii. 15, the pl. signifies the sides, &c., of the earth: (Fr:) or its roads, accord. to some: (TA:) or its mountains: (Zj:) which last signification in this case is preferred by Az: (TA:) or the sing. signifies an elevated place, or part, of the earth or land. (S.) ― -b7- AlmanaAkibN (tropical:) The feathers next after the qawaAdim ; [which latter are the anterior, or primary, feathers of a bird's wing;] (K;) the feathers of the wing of a vulture or an eagle that are next after the qwAdm , which are the strongest and most excellent of the feathers; (TA:) four [ feathers ] in the wing of a bird, next after the qwAdm (S.) [ the four secondary feathers of the wing: ] in the wing of a bird are twenty leathers: the first of them are those called AlqwAdm ; the next, AlmnAkb ; the next, AlxawaA fiY : the next, AlA^abAhiru ; the next, AlkulaY . (L.) It is a word without a sing. (K.) ISd says, I know not a sing. to it; but by analogy it should be manokibN . (TA.) ― -b8- sahomahu bimanaAkiba rAa$a (tropical:) He feathered his arrow with feathers such as are described above. (TA.) -A2- manokibN (tropical:) EariyfN i. q. The intendant, superintendent, &c., of a people or an aider, helper, or assistant, of a people: (K:) or the assistant of an Eryf : (Msb:) one below an Eryf : (IAth:) or the chief of the EurafaA'u [pl. of Eryf ]; (Lth, S:) there being over so many ErfA' a mnkb . (Lth [see EariyfN .]) pl. manaAkibu . (TA.)

definition: , pl. A^anowaA='N and nuwA=nN , (S, K,) A star, or an asterism, verging to setting: or the setting of the star, or asterism, in the west, aurorally, i. e., at dawn of morning, and the rising of...
sourceDefinition: , pl. A^anowaA='N and nuwA=nN , (S, K,) A star, or an asterism, verging to setting: or the setting of the star, or asterism, in the west, aurorally, i. e., at dawn of morning, and the rising of another, opposite to it, at the same time, in the east: (K:) or the setting of one of the stars, or asterisms, which compose the Mansions [ of the Moon (see manaAzilu Alqamari )], in the west, aurorally, i. e., at dawn of morining, and the rising of its raqiyb , which is another star, or asterism, opposite to it, at the same time, in the east, each night for a period of thirteen days: thus does each star, or asterism, of those Mansions, [one after another,] to the end of the year, except Aljabohap , the period of which is fourteen days: (S:) [or it signifies the auroral rising, and sometimes the auroral setting, of one of those stars, or asterisms; as will be shown below: I do not say “ heliacal ” rising because the rising here meant continues for a period of thirteen days]. Accord. to the T, nw' signifies the setting of one of the stars, or asterisms, above mentioned: and AHn says, that it signifies its first setting in the morning, when the stars are about to disappear; which is when the whiteness of dawn diffuses itself. (TA.) A'Obeyd says, I have not heard nw' used in the sense of “ setting, ” “ falling, ” except in this instance. (S.) It is added, [whether on his or another's authority is doubtful,] that the [pagan] Arabs used to attribute the rains and winds and heat and cold to such of the stars, or asterisms, above mentioned as was setting at the time [ aurorally ]; or, accord. to As, to that which was rising in its ascendency [ aurorally ]; and used to say, muTironaA binawo'i ka*aA [ We have been given rain by such a nw' ]; (S;) or they attributed heat [and cold] to the rising or the star or asterism, and rain [and wind], to its nawo' [meaning its setting ]. (AHn, Har, p. 216.) This the Muslim is forbidden to say, unless he mean thereby, “ We have been given rain at the period of such a nw' ; ” God having made it usual for rain to come at [certain of] the periods called AnwA' . Again, A'Obeyd says, The AnwA' are twenty-eight stars, or asterisms; sing. nw' : the rising of any one of them in the east [ aurorally ] is called nw' ; and the star, or asterism, itself is hence thus called: but sometimes nw' signifies the setting. Also, in the L it is said, that each of the abovementioned stars, or asterisms, is called thus because, when that in the west sets, the opposite one rises; and this rising is called Aln~w' ; but some make nw' to signify the setting; as if it bore contr. senses. (TA.) [El-Kazweenee mentions certain physical occurrences on the occasions of the AnwA' of the Mansions of the Moon; and in each of these cases, except three, the nw' is the rising, not the setting. Two of the excepted cases are doubtful: the passage relating to the third plainly expresses an event which happens at the period of the auroral setting of AlS~arofap ; namely the commencement of the days called A^ay~aAmu AlEajuwzi ; corresponding, accord. to ElMakreezee, with the rising of Alfarogu Almuqad~amu , the rqyb of AlSrfp : and it is said in the S, art. Ejz , on the authority of Ibn-Kunáseh, that the Ay~Am AlEjwz fall at the period of the nw' of AlSrfp . (The auroral setting of AlSrfp , at the commencement of the era of the Flight, in central Arabia, happened about the 9th of March O. S.; and this is the day of the N. S., the 26th of February O. S., on which commence the Ay~Am AlEjwz accord. to the modern Egyptian almanacs.) Hence it appears, that sometimes the setting, but generally the rising, was called the nw' . Moreover, the ancient Arabs had twenty-eight proverbial sayings (which are quoted in the Mir-át ez-Zemán, and in the work of El-Kazweenee) relating to the risings of the twenty-eight Mansions of the Moon: such as this: A_i*aA TalaEa Al$~araTaAno A_isotawaY Alz~amaAno “ When Esh-Sharatán rises, the season becomes temperate: ” or, perhaps, “ ― -b2- the night and day, become equal. ” (If this latter meaning could be proved to be the right one, we might infer that the Calendar of the Mansions of the Moon was in use more than twelve centuries B. c.; and that for this reason Al$rTAn was called the first of the mansions; though it may have been first so called at a later period as being the first Mansion in the first Sign of the Zodiac. But I return to the more immediate object which I had in view in mentioning the foregoing sayings.) I do not find any of these sayings (though others, I believe, do) relating to the settings. sourceDefinition: , (Msb,) and nayoluwfarN , (Msb, and so in the CK,) or nayolawofarN , (so in copies of the K, and so accord. to the TA,) or, as some say, nayonuwfarN , or nayonuwofarN , (accord. to different copies of the K,) [The nymphæa, or lotus of Egypt and of Syria; ] a certain well-known plant; (Msb;) a kind of sweet-smelling plant, which grows in stagnant waters, (K, TA,) called by the people of Egypt b$nyn , [i. e. ba$oniyn ,] and by the vulgar nawofar ; (TA;) [both of which last names are now given in Egypt to the nymphæa lotus, or white lotus, found in the neighbourhoods of Rosetta and Damietta; and the former, also, or perhaps both, to the nymphæa cærulea, or blue lotus, found in the same parts, and, until within a few years, in a lake on the north of Cairo, called Birket erRatlee, whence I have twice procure roots of this plant:] nylwfr [written in Persian niyloParo and niyluwParo and niyluwbaroko &c.] is a Persian word ( A^aEojamiy~apN ), and is said to be composed of niyl , [or indigo,] with which one dyes, and the name for a wing, [i. e., Paro ;] as though “ winged with niyl [or indigo]; ” because the leaf is as though its two wings were dyed [with indigo]: (Msb:) the plant so called is cold in the third degree, moist in the second degree, emollient, good for cough and for pains of the side and lungs and chest; when its root, or lower part, ( A^aSol ,) is kneaded with water, and used as a liniment, several times, it removes the disease called Albahaq ; and when kneaded with zifot , it removes the disease called daA='u Alv~aEolabi : (K, TA:) an excellent beverage is also prepared from it. (TA.) The imám Bedred-Deen Mudhaffar, son of the Kádee of Baalabekk, says, in his book entitled Suroor en-Nefs, that it is of many species; whereof [one or more] in Syria, used in perfume; and a species in Egypt, blue; and that its temperament is cold and moist in the second degree; that the smelling it is useful against hot diseases, and anxiety; and its juice in like manner; and that the beverage prepared from it is useful as a remedy for cough and roughness [of the throat] and pain of the side and chest, and is a laxative. The author of the Irshád and that of the Moojiz also mention, that the beverage prepared from it is an exception from other sweet beverages inasmuch as it does not become converted into yellow bile, which is wonderful; and its oil is more cold and moist than that of violets; and there is no flower more cold and moist than it. Er-Rázee, too, says that the smelling it is one of the causes of weakening the generative faculty, and that the beverage is one of the causes of stopping it; [for which purpose, or as an antiaphrodisiac, it is used in the present day by some of the women of Cairo;] notwithstanding which, it rejoices the heart, and is useful for palpitation of the heart. This art. is omitted by J and Sgh and the author of the L. (TA.)

definition: A certain plant;
sourceDefinition: A certain plant; (S, K;) when it dries, it becomes red; and when it is eaten, and grows, it is called jamiymN : or, accord. to Az, a certain tree, growing like the Sil~iyaAn , except that its colour inclines to red: or, accord. to Aboo-Ziyád, as AHn says, a plant of the kind called Tariyfap , growing like the Sl~yAn and the naSiY~ , red when fresh and moist, and more red when it has dried: it is watery; and the camels and sheep &c. scarcely ever eat it when they find any other herbage to serve them in its stead. (TA.)

sourceDefinition: , aor. yajidu and yajudu , (S, L, Msb, K,) the latter of the dial. of the tribe of 'Ámir (S, L, Msb) Ibn-Saasa'ah, (MF,) and without a parallel (S, L, Msb, K) in verbs of this class, (S, L, Msb,) the w in it being dropped because it falls out in the original form of the aor., (Msb,) both of which forms are said by several authors to apply to the verb in all its significations, though F seems to restrict the latter to two significations, (TA,) inf. n. wujuwdN (S, L, Msb, K) and wijodaAn (L, Msb, K,) and A_ijodaAnN , (IAar, L, K,) in which the w is changed into ' , (L,) and wajodN and wujodN and jidapN ; (L, K;) and wajidahu , aor. yajidu ; (K;) but this form of the verb is not found in the lexicons, [the K only accepted,] (MF,) in the sense here assigned to it; (TA;) He found it; lighted on it; attained it; obtained it by searching or seeking; discovered it; perceived it; saw it; experienced it, or became sensible of it; (F, in the K and in the Basáïr, on the authority of Abu-l-Kásim El-Isbahánee;) namely, a thing sought, sought for or after, or desired; (S, L, K;) and simply a thing. (L.) wujuwd is of several kinds. It is The finding, &c., by means of any one of the five senses: as when one says wajadotu zayodFA [ I found, &c., Zeyd ]: and wajadatu TaEomahu , and raAy^iHatahu , and Sawotahu , and xu$uwnatahu , [ I found, or perceived, &c., its taste, and its odour, and its sound, and its roughness ]. Also, The finding, &c., by means of the faculty of appetite, [ or rather of sensation, which is the cause of appetite:] as when one says wajadotu Al$~ibaEa [ I found, experienced, or became sensible of, satiety ]. Also, The finding, &c., by the intellect, or by means of the intellect: of which kind is one's knowing God: and here it should be observed, that wjwd attributed to God is simple knowledge: (Abu-l-Kásim El-Isbahánee, cited in the Basáïr:) wajada A@ll~`hu , wherever it occurs, means God knew. (Er-Rághib, Z, &c.) i. e., in the Kur-án. (TA.) ― -b2- wajada [ He found, in the sense of ] he knew [ by experience ]. (A, TA, &c.) [In this sense, it is a verb of the kind called A^afoEaAlu Alquluwbi ; having two objective complements; the first of which is called its noun, and the second its predicate.] Ex. wajadotu zayodFA *aA AlHifaAZi I [ found, or] knew Zeyd to possess the quality of defending those things which should be sacred, or inviolable. (A.) Used in this sense, as doubly trans., its inf. n. is wajodaAnN (Akh) and wujuwdN . (Seer.) It is also used as singly trans., as syn. with Ealima . (TA.) ― -b3- When wajada signifies he found, or lighted on, a thing after it had gone away, its inf. n. is wijodaAnN . (IKtt.) ― -b4- wajada AlD~aAl~apa , (S, A, Msb,) aor. yajid (Msb) and yajudu , (MF,) inf. n. wajodaAnN (S, Msb) and lamo A^ajido mino *`lika bud~FA (Msb) [ He found the stray beast ]. ― -b5- lamo A^ajido mino *`lika bud~FA , for which one also says lamo Ajdi , I found no means of avoiding, or escaping, that. (Kz, TA.) ― -b6- wajada , (L,) and wajada fiY AlmaAli , (Fs, T, S, L, Msb,) and wajada AlmaAla wagayarahu , (Lh, M, K,) aor. yajidu , (Lh, M, L, K,) inf. n. wujod and wijd and wajodN and jidahN (Lh, T, S, M, K) and wijodaAnN (T, L) and wujuwdN , (Yz,) He became possessed of wealth, or property: (T:) or he was, or became, rich; possessed of competence, or sufficiency; in no need; without wants, or with few wants; (S, M, L, K;) so as not to be poor afterwards: (L:) and he gained, acquired, or earned wealth. (Exps. of the Fs.) Hence the saying of the Arabs, wijodaAnu Alr~aqiyni yugaT~iY A^afana AlA^afiyni [ The possession of money hides the weakness of judgment of the weak in judgment ]. (T, L.) -A2- wajada Ealayohi , (S, L, K, &c.) aor. yajidu (Fs, M, L, K) and yajudu ; (M, L, K;) and wajida , as heard by Fr from certain of the Arabs; (Kzz;) inf. n. mawojidapN , (Fs, S, A, L, Msb, K,) by some pronounced mawojadapN , (Fr,) and wajodN and jidapN (L, K) and wijodaAnN (Lh, S, M, L) and wujuwdN (Fr, Kzz) He was angry with him: (Fs, S, A, L, Msb, K) or he was angry with him with the anger that proceeds from a friend. (TA, voce EatobN .) -A3- wajada bihi , (aor. yajidu , L,) inf. n. wajodN , He loved him. (L, K.) wajada bihaA , (A, L,) and ↓ tw~jd , (A,) He loved her; (A, L;) he loved her passionately or fondly. (L.) lahu bihaA wajodN He has a love [or passionate or fond love ] for her. (A.) -A4- wajada , [aor. yajidu ,] ('Eyn, Fs, S, L, Msb, &c.,) and wajida , [aor. yawojadu ,] (El-Hejeree, M, K,) the latter the only form mentioned in the K, but the former is the only form generally known, (MF, TA,) and wajuda , (Lh, M, L,) inf. n. wajodN , (S, L, Msb, K, &c.,) He grieved; mourned; sorrowed. (S, L, Msb, K, &c.) You say, wajadotu bihi , (Msb,) and lahu ↓ twj~dt , (S, L,) I grieved, mourned, or sorrowed, for such a one. (S, L, Msb.) Ibn-Hishám El-Lakhmee says, that in this sense wjd is not transitive: (MF:) [i. e., without a prep.]. -A5- wujida , (inf. n. wujuwdN , A, Msb,) It existed; it became existent (A, Msb) from a state of nonexistence. (S, L, K.)

(Er-Rághib, Z, &c.) i. e., in the Kur-án. (TA.) ― -b2- wajada [ He found, in the sense of ] he knew [ by experience ]. (A, TA, &c.) [In this sense, it is a verb of the kind called A^afoEaAlu Alquluwbi ; having two objective complements; the first of which is called its noun, and the second its predicate.] Ex. wajadotu zayodFA *aA AlHifaAZi I [ found, or] knew Zeyd to possess the quality of defending those things which should be sacred, or inviolable. (L.) ― -b5- layolapN warodapN (tropical:) A night of which the beginning and end are red; which is the case in a time of drought. (A.) ― -b6- warodN Bold, or daring; (K;) an epithet applied to a man; (TA;) as also ↓ waAridN . (K.) ― -b7- warodN Saffron. definition: A coming to, or arriving at, water &c.
sourceDefinition: A coming to, or arriving at, water &c., whether one enters it or does not enter it; (S, * L, Msb, K;) contr. of SadarN . (S, L, Msb.) See also 1. ― -b2- wirodN Water to which one comes to drink. (L.) ― -b3- wirodN The time of the day of coming to water, between the two periods of abstaining from water: (L:) a time, or turn, of coming to water. (TA in art. Hzb .) ― -b4- wirodN The arrival of the day of coming to water. (L.) ― -b5- waradati AlA_ibilu AlmaA='a wirodFA , and A^aworaAdF , and in like manner, AlT~ayoru , The camels, and the birds, came to the water in a herd, or in a flock, and in herds, or in flocks. (L.) ― -b6- wir~dN A company of men, (S, L, Msb, K,) and a number of camels, and of birds, &c., (L,) coming to, or arriving at, water; (S, L, Msb, K;) as also ↓ waAridapN : (L, Msb, K:) the former originally an inf. n.: (Msb:) its pl. is A^aworaAdN . (L.) See also waAridN . ― -b7- wirodN A herd of camels. (L.) ― -b8- A flock of birds. (L, K.) ― -b9- (tropical:) An army, (L, K,) so called as being likened to a herd of camels, or to a flock of birds. (L.) ― -b10- A portion, or share, of water. (L, K.) ― -b11- Thirst. (L.) ― -b12- nasuwqu Almujorimiyna A_ilaY jahay~ama wirodFA [Kur, xix, 89,] (assumed tropical:) We will drive the sinners to hell like beasts that come to water: or, thirsty: (Beyd:) or, walking and thirsty. (Zj, L.) ― -b13- wirodN (tropical:) The day of a fever, when it attacks the patient periodically: (As, S, L, Msb, * K *:) or one of the names of fever: (L, K:) but the former explanation is the more correct. (TA.) ― -b14- wirodN (assumed tropical:) A portion of the night when a man has to pray. (L.) ― -b15- wirodN (tropical:) A section, or division, (S, L, K,) of the Kur-án: (L, K:) a set portion of recitation or the like: (Msb:) a certain portion of the Kur-án, as a seventh, or half a seventh, or the like, (Mgh, L,) which a person recites at a particular time: (L:) a set portion of the Kur-án, or of prayer; &c., of which a man imposes upon himself the recital on a particular occasion, or at a particular time; i. q. HizobN q. v.: (Mgh, L:) pl. A^aworaAdN . (L, Msb.) Ex. qaraA^otu wirodiY [ I recited my set portion of the Kur-án, &c. ]: (S, L:) and lifulaAnK kul~a layolapK wirodN mina AlquroA=ni yaqoraA^uhu Such a one has every night a set portion of the Kur-án which he recites. (L.)

sourceDefinition: , and Habolu Alwariydi , [ Each of the two carotid arteries: and sometimes applied to each of the two external jugular veins: ] each of two veins asserted by the Arabs to be from the watiyn [or aorta ], on the right and left of the two sides of the neck, next the fore part, and thick: (S, L:) or the wryd is a certain vein, said to be the wadaj [or external jugular vein ]: or, by the side of the wdj : or, accord. to Fr, a certain vein between the windpipe and [ the two sinews called ] the EilobaAwaAni , always pulsing; being one of the veins in which is the life; the blood not flowing in it, but only the soul, Alnfs [i. e., Aln~afosu , not Aln~afasu ; for, accord. to the Arabs, the animal soul ( Alr~uwHu AlHayowaAniY~u , as is said in the KT,) diffuses itself throughout the body, from the heart, by means of the pulsing veins, or arteries: see also wadajN ]: (Msb:) or the wariydaAni are two veins in the neck, (AZ, L, K,) between the A^awodaAj [or external jugular veins ] and [ the two parts of the neck called ] the liytaAni : in the camel, the wadajaAni [or two external jugular veins ]: (AZ, T:) or, accord. to AHeyth, and his is the correct explanation, two veins beneath the wadajaAni , [see above,] which latter are two thick veins on the right and left of the pit between the clavicles; they (the former) are always pulsing, in man: the wryd is a vein in which the soul ( Alnfs [see above]) flows, and in which the blood does not flow: and every pulsing vein, in which the life flows, is of those thus called: (T:) or the wryd is the vein in each side of the neck which swells out on an occasion of anger: (L:) or four veins in the head; of which two descend before the ears, and of which are the wrydAn in the neck: or a certain vein beneath the tongue: and, in the upper half of the arm, the faliyq [or cephalic ]: and, in the fore arm, the A^akoHal [or median ]: and, among those which separate in the outer side of the hand, the A^a$aAjiE : and, in the belly of the fore arm, the rawaAhi$ : (T:) pl. A^aworidapN [a pl. of pauc.] (M, Msb, K) and warudN , (M, Msb,) like as burudN is pl. of bariydN , (Msb,) [and wutunN of watiynN , &c.,] or waruwdN , (K,) [but this I think a mistake]. ― -b2- rajulN munotafixu Alwariydi [ A man whose external jugular vein swells out; ] a man of bad disposition or temper, prone to anger. (TA.)

definition: He preserved, or guarded, himself exceedingly, or extraordinarily: (Ksh, Bd in ii.
sourceDefinition: He preserved, or guarded, himself exceedingly, or extraordinarily: (Ksh, Bd in ii. 1:) he put a thing between him and another to preserve him, or guard him. (Ham, p. 359.) ― -b2- In the conventional language of the law, He preserved, or guarded, himself exceedingly, or extraordinarily, (Ksh, Bd, ubi supra,) from sin, of commission or of omission, (Ksh,) [or] from what would harm him in the world to come. (Bd, who describes three degrees.) It may often be rendered He was pious; or careful of his religious duties. ― -b3- Ait~aqaY Ealayohimo waHa*ira [ He guarded himself against them in an extraordinary degree, and was cautious, or wary ]. (JK, TA, in art. x$Y .) See 1. ― -b4- yatoqiY , for yat~aqiY : see art. tqY : and see a verse of Khufáf Ibn-Nudbeh, (quoted in the S, in art. wqY ,) cited voce A^avorN . ― -b5- yat~aqo for yat~aqi : see a verse cited voce mutaA^aw~ibN .
